Sanskrit is the classical language of ancient India, an Indo-Aryan language of the Indo-European family. It was the sacred language of Hinduism and the main language of learning across South Asia and much of Southeast Asia for some two thousand years.

Its oldest form, Vedic Sanskrit, is the language of the Rigveda and the other Vedas, composed during the Vedic period from about 1500 BCE. Around the 4th century BCE the grammarian Pāṇini described the language in a set of nearly four thousand rules. His work fixed the form now called Classical Sanskrit.

In it were written the epics Mahabharata and Ramayana, the plays and poems of Kalidasa, law books, works of medicine, mathematics and astronomy, and many Mahayana Buddhist texts. Kings used it for their inscriptions from about the 2nd century CE, and the habit spread overseas: the Yupa inscriptions of Kutai in Borneo are in Sanskrit, and Khmer and Javanese courts wrote in it too. Kashmir's history, the Rajatarangini, is in Sanskrit verse.

Everyday speech moved on into the Prakrits and later into languages such as Hindi, Bengali and Marathi, but Sanskrit stayed alive as a learned language. Outsiders who wanted to understand India learned it, from al-Biruni in the 11th century to the scholars of the Asiatic Society. In 1786 William Jones pointed out that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin must share a common source, which started the study of the Indo-European languages.
